Alcoholic number 3 Bill Dodson, is 12 stepped on June 28, 1935. “On the third day the lawyer gave his life to the care and direction of his Creator, and said he was perfectly willing to do anything necessary.” “He never drank again.”

Throughout our book we are directed to get into action, our program is one of urgency. The sooner we place ourselves in the loving care of our Creator the sooner we recover and stop hurting those around us.

All too often I hear members telling newcomers to take it easy. I like to ask them what they would do if they had a gunshot wound and the doctor recommended taking it easy, just keep coming back, it will get better… don’t make any changes for a year. Have some coffee and tell me how bad it hurts so that I can remember the pain and not have to get shot again! Oh and no matter what you do JUST DON’T BLEED! No matter what... if you start to think you are going to bleed get yourself to a meeting and talk about it.
We turn to God for help and get saved we don’t get our life in order then turn to God.
Anyone care to fill us in about the “devil-may-care young fellow”?

“He suffered horribly from his sprees, but it seemed as if nothing could be done for him. He consented, however, to go to the hospital, where he occupied the very room recently vacated by the lawyer.
He had three visitors. After a bit, he said, "The way you fellows put this spiritual stuff makes sense. I'm ready to do business. I guess the old folks were right after all." So one more was added to the Fellowship.
All this time our friend of the hotel lobby incident remained in that town. He was there three months. He now returned home, leaving behind his first acquaintance, the lawyer and the devil-may-care chap. These men had found something brand new in life. Though they knew they must help other alcoholics if they would remain sober, that motive became secondary. It was transcended by the happiness they found in giving themselves for others. They shared their homes, their slender resources, and gladly devoted their spare hours to fellow-sufferers. They were willing, by day or night, to place a new man in the hospital and visit him afterward. They grew in numbers. They experienced a few distressing failures, but in those cases they made an effort to bring the man's family into a spiritual way of living, thus relieving much worry and suffering.
A year and six months later these three had succeeded with seven more. Seeing much of each other, scarce an evening passed that someone's home did not shelter a little gathering of men and women, happy in their release, and constantly thinking how they might present their discovery to some newcomer. In addition to these casual get-togethers, it became customary to set apart one night a week for a meeting to be attended by anyone or everyone interested in a spiritual way of life.”
“one more was added to the Fellowship.” Alcoholic number 4 was Ernie Galbraith he was married to Dr. Bob's daughter Sue.
Bill W. remained in Akron for three months. In September Bill returns home and AA begins in NYC. Dr. Bob, Bill Dodson and Ernie Galbraith go to work in and around Akron.

“These men had found something brand new in life. Though they knew they must help other alcoholics if they would remain sober, that motive became secondary. It was transcended by the happiness they found in giving themselves for others.”

“They shared their homes, their slender resources, and gladly devoted their spare hours to fellow-sufferers. They were willing, by day or night, to place a new man in the hospital and visit him afterward. They grew in numbers. They experienced a few distressing failures, but in those cases they made an effort to bring the man's family into a spiritual way of living, thus relieving much worry and suffering.”
I can only imagine the joy and disappointments our founders experienced, thank God for their commitment and tireless charity.
“it became customary to set apart one night a week for a meeting to be attended by anyone or everyone interested in a spiritual way of life.”

One night a week was set aside for meetings for “anyone or everyone interested in a spiritual way of life” the rest of their time was spent meeting for prayer, meditation and service to others and carrying our message to others.

Anyone notice any difference between then and now? My fear is that if alcoholics anonymous does not experience a rebirth of spirit and camaraderie, alcoholics anonymous will continue to decline and we will perish. I pray that I am seeing this wrong.
The question I ask myself today is “what have I done TODAY to contribute to our fellowship and help a fellow alcoholic”

“Aside from fellowship and sociability, the prime object was to provide a time and place where new people might bring their problems.
Outsiders became interested. One man and his wife placed their large home at the disposal of this strangely assorted crowd. This couple has since become so fascinated that they have dedicated their home to the work. Many a distracted wife has visited this house to find loving and understanding companionship among women who knew her problem, to hear from the lips of their husbands what had happened to them, to be advised how her own wayward mate might be hospitalized and approached when next he stumbled.
Many a man, yet dazed from his hospital experience, has stepped over the threshold of that home into freedom. Many an alcoholic who entered there came away with an answer. He succumbed to that gay crowd inside, who laughed at their own misfortunes and understood his. Impressed by those who visited him at the hospital, he capitulated entirely when, later, in an upper room of this house, he heard the story of some man whose experience closely tallied with his own. The expression on the faces of the women, that indefinable something in the eyes of the men, the stimulating and electric atmosphere of the place, conspired to let him know that here was haven at last.
The very practical approach to his problems, the absence of intolerance of any kind, the informality, the genuine democracy, the uncanny understanding which these people had were irresistible. He and his wife would leave elated by the thought of what they could now do for some stricken acquaintance and his family.”
Our book says our founders stayed in contact with one another and were constantly thinking how they might present our program to some newcomer.

In addition to casual get-togethers, they set apart one night a week for a meeting to be attended. “Aside from fellowship and sociability, the prime object was to provide a time and place where new people might bring their problems.” Based on our book and my limited knowledge of our history I believe the basic answer to the problems presented would have been directions on how to apply our principles to daily life, and using perceived problems as an opportunity to practice these principles. and once again we are reminded that offering our way of life to others is the core of our program "He and his wife would leave elated by the thought of what they could now do for some stricken acquaintance and his family.”
Here is a link to a story of early aa meetings and some information on the man and his wife who offered the use of their home:
http://www.silkworth.net/chs/chs0307.html
Am I using and offering “a practical approach” to problems with the “absence of intolerance of any kind” and understanding fellowship.

“They knew they had a host of new friends; it seemed they had known these strangers always. They had seen miracles, and one was to come to them. They had visioned the Great Reality - their loving and All Powerful Creator.
Now, this house will hardly accommodate its weekly visitors, for they number sixty or eighty as a rule. Alcoholics are being attracted from far and near. From surrounding towns, families drive long distances to be present. A community thirty miles away has fifteen fellows of Alcoholics Anonymous. Being a large place, we think that some day its Fellowship will number many hundreds.
But life among Alcoholics Anonymous is more than attending gatherings and visiting hospitals. Cleaning up old scrapes, helping to settle family differences, explaining the disinherited son to his irate parents, lending money and securing jobs for each other, when justified - these are everyday occurrences. No one is too discredited or has sunk too low to be welcomed cordially - if he means business. Social distinctions, petty rivalries and jealousies - these are laughed out of countenance. Being wrecked in the same vessel, being restored and united under one God, with hearts and minds attuned to the welfare of others, the things which matter so much to some people no longer signify much to them. How could they?”

The “Great Reality - their loving and All Powerful Creator” I know little about my Creator, what I do know is this Higher Power seems to be like a loving parent, no matter what I have done I am always in its grace, I don’t have to work at gaining this love – it is always there. I don’t always get what I want but it appears I get what is best for me. I am given the freedom of leaving at anytime and at anytime I may return to this loving grace.

A community thirty miles away – would be Cleveland Ohio where alcoholic Clarence Snyder broke away from the Oxford group meetings in Akron and started AA in Cleveland on May 18, 1939 at the Cleveland Heights home of Abby G. It is said that this was the first group to be called "Alcoholics Anonymous” by all I have read Clarence was a fundamentalist who worked tirelessly promoting alcoholics anonymous. I understand there are mixed opinions on the work Clarence and some of his sponsees have carried forth. Anyone have information on this?

What do we do? - attend gatherings, visiting hospitals. Clean up old scrapes, helping to settle family differences, explaining the alcoholic symptoms and program to families, lending money and securing jobs for each other, when justified.
A guiding point – “No one is too discredited or has sunk too low to be welcomed cordially”
Question - who am I to know if he means business? And how am I to know if he means business?
“Social distinctions, petty rivalries and jealousies - these are laughed out of countenance.”
Was I wrecked and now restored? Am I united under one God? Is my heart and mind attuned to the welfare of others? Do worldly things still mean too much to me?

“Under only slightly different conditions, the same thing is taking place in many eastern cities. In one of these there is a well-known hospital for the treatment of alcoholic and drug addiction. Six years ago one of our number was a patient there. Many of us have felt, for the first time, the Presence and Power of God within its walls. We are greatly indebted to the doctor in attendance there, for he, although it might prejudice his own work, has told us of his belief in ours.
Every few days this doctor suggests our approach to one of his patients. Understanding our work, he can do this with an eye to selecting those who are willing and able to recover on a spiritual basis. Many of us, former patients, go there to help. Then, in this eastern city, there are informal meetings such as we have described to you, where you may now see scores of members. There are the same fast friendships, there is the same helpfulness to one another as you find among our western friends. There is a good bit of travel between East and West and we foresee a great increase in this helpful interchange.
Some day we hope that every alcoholic who journeys will find a Fellowship of Alcoholics Anonymous at his destination. To some extent this is already true. Some of us are salesmen and go about. Little clusters of twos and threes and fives of us have sprung up in other communities, through contact with our two larger centers. Those of us who travel drop in as often as we can. This practice enables us to lend a hand, at the same time avoiding certain alluring distractions of the road, about which any traveling man can inform you.
Thus we grow. And so can you, though you be but one man with this book in your hand. We believe and hope it contains all you will need to begin.”

“Under only slightly different conditions” I am not sure but they may be talking about the difference between the Akron and Cincinnati groups tendency to keep our program God and bible based and NY using a more psychological approach.

Anyone know who the salesmen were? “Some of us are salesmen and go about.” I seem to remember one that worked for the car wax company and didn’t believe in God the group kept sending out on the road to avoid his protests.
Do I help AA to grow? And do I believe that this book contains all I need to begin? Have I begun - today?

“We know what you are thinking. You are saying to yourself: "I'm jittery and alone. I couldn't do that." But you can. You forget that you have just now tapped a source of power much greater than yourself. To duplicate, with such backing, what we have accomplished is only a matter of willingness, patience and labor.
We know of an A.A. member who was living in a large community. He had lived there but a few weeks when he found that the place probably contained more alcoholics per square mile than any city in the country. This was only a few days ago at this writing. (1939) The authorities were much concerned. He got in touch with a prominent psychiatrist who had undertaken certain responsibilities for the mental health of the community. The doctor proved to be able and exceedingly anxious to adopt any workable method of handling the situation. So he inquired, what did our friend have on the ball?
Our friend proceeded to tell him. And with such good effect that the doctor agreed to a test among his patients and certain other alcoholics from a clinic which he attends. Arrangements were also made with the chief psychiatrist of a large public hospital to select still others from the stream of misery which flows through that institution.
So our fellow worker will soon have friends galore. Some of them may sink and perhaps never get up, but if our experience is a criterion, more than half of those approached will become fellows of Alcoholics Anonymous.”
Have I tapped a source of power much greater than myself?
Do my actions confirm that?
Do my actions demonstrate willingness, patience and labor?
Our History:
The “A.A. member who was living in a large community” was Hank Parkhurst he lived in Morris Plains, NJ.
I have seen two names associated with the “prominent psychiatrist.”
Dr. James Wainwright Howard from Montclair, helped edit the original manuscript of our book - http://hindsfoot.org/docu1.html
Greystone Park Psychiatric Hospital is about 30 minutes away, which would leave Dr. Marcus Curry, (superintendent of Greystone) as the prominent psychiatrist.
The history of alcoholics anonymous is rich, hundreds of unsung heroes who gave time and energy to develop our program and grow our fellowship. We have been saved because of their tireless work.

At times I am complacent in AA, my prayers and service become superficial. Our founders warned us, “It is easy to let up on the spiritual program of action“. If we are to survive we must not become complacent.
Dr. Bob summarized - our program, when boiled down, is love and service. He warned us to keep it simple. I pray that I keep it simple and maintain the roots of what alcoholics anonymous is.

“When a few men in this city have found themselves, and have discovered the joy of helping others to face life again, there will be no stopping until everyone in that town has had his opportunity to recover - if he can and will.
Still you may say: "But I will not have the benefit of contact with you who write this book." We cannot be sure. God will determine that, so you must remember that your real reliance is always upon Him. He will show you how to create the fellowship you crave.
Our book is meant to be suggestive only. We realize we know only a little. God will constantly disclose more to you and to us. Ask Him in your morning meditation what you can do each day for the man who is still sick. The answers will come, if your own house is in order. But obviously you cannot transmit something you haven't got. See to it that your relationship with Him is right, and great events will come to pass for you and countless others. This is the Great Fact for us.
Abandon yourself to God as you understand God. Admit your faults to Him and to your fellows. Clear away the wreckage of your past. Give freely of what you find and join us. We shall be with you in the Fellowship of the Spirit, and you will surely meet some of us as you trudge the Road of Happy Destiny.
May God bless you and keep you - until then.”
Have I found my true self? Have I found the joy have of helping others? Will I help those I encounter have an opportunity to recover?
Am I developing the fellowship that I crave?
“Our book is meant to be suggestive only. We realize we know only a little.” This is a statement of humility, followed by a promise and direction if we want to have it fulfilled.
Am I asking God in my morning meditation what I can do each day for the man who is still sick?
Am I doing what I can for the man who is still sick?
Is my house is in order?
Am I working on my relationship with God?
Am I spreading our message?
If I take these actions great events will come to pass for me, my family and countless others. This is the Great Fact for us.
Abandon yourself to God as you understand God. We do that in Steps 1, 2 &3
Admit your faults to Him and to your fellows. We do that in 4, 5, 6 & 7
Clear away the wreckage of your past. We do that in 8 &9
Give freely of what you find and join us. We do that in 10, 11 & 12

I think this passage may hint of another fellowship, a fellowship of the spirit that I enter after I have abandoned myself to God, admitted my faults to Him and my fellows, worked to clear the wreckage of my past and start giving freely of what I have been so freely given.
So I have the option of joining the fellowship and attending meetings as well as joining a fellowship of the spirit and sharing our common solution.

days.title: Personal Stories · How the Stories Are Arranged

items.x: How Forty-Three Alcoholics
Recovered From Their Malady"
Beginning with the story of “Dr. Bob,” a co-founder of A.A., there are here presented three groups of personal histories.
Part I
PIONEERS OF A.A.
This group of thirteen stories shows that sobriety in A.A. can be lasting.
Part II
THEY STOPPED IN TIME
Seventeen stories may help you decide whether you are alcoholic; also, whether A.A. is for you.
Part III
THEY LOST NEARLY ALL
Those who believe their drinking to be hopeless may again find hope in these thirteen impressive tales.

I think it is important to understand how our book was laid out. If I am to learn from the stories I may want to understand what worked and for who. The pioneers refined our program, helped those who stopped in time as well as those who nearly lost all.
A co-founder of Alcoholics Anonymous. The birth of our society dates from his first day of permanent sobriety, June 10 1935.
To 1950, the year of his death, he carried the A.A. message to more than 5,000 alcoholic men and women, and to all these he gave his medical services without thought of charge.
In this prodigy of service, he was well assisted by Sister Ignatia at St. Thomas Hospital in Akron, Ohio, one of the greatest friends our Fellowship will ever know."

“I was born in a small New England village of about seven thousand souls. The general moral standard was, as I recall it, far above the average. No beer or liquor was sold in the neighborhood, except at the State liquor agency where perhaps one might procure a pint if he could convince the agent that he really needed it. Without this proof the expectant purchaser would be forced to depart empty handed with none of what I later came to believe was the great panacea for all human ills. Men who had liquor shipped in from Boston or New York by express were looked upon with great distrust and disfavor by most of the good townspeople. The town was well supplied with churches and schools in which I pursued my early educational activities.
My father was a professional man of recognized ability and both my father and mother were most active in church affairs. Both father and mother were considerably above the average in intelligence.”
Dr. Bob was raised in what looks like a normal “above average” home and community. Beer and liquor where not readily available and were looked upon with disfavor.

Dr. Bob was known as the “The Prince of All Twelfth Steppers” he carried the message of alcoholics anonymous to over 5000 men and women. By my math that’s about 1 a day, that’s quite a standard, thank God for his love and commitment to our way of life.

“Unfortunately for me, I was the only child, which perhaps engendered the selfishness which played such an important part in bringing on my alcoholism. From childhood through high school I was more or less forced to go to church, Sunday School and evening service, Monday night Christian Endeavor and sometimes to Wednesday evening prayer meeting. This had the effect of making me resolve that when I was free from parental domination, I would never again darken the doors of a church. This resolution I kept steadfastly for the next forty years, except when circumstances made it seem unwise to absent myself.
After high school came four years in one of the best colleges in the country where drinking seemed to be a major extra-curricular activity. Almost everyone seemed to do it. I did it more and more, and had lots of fun without much grief, either physical or financial. I seemed to be able to snap back the next morning better than most of my fellow drinkers, who were cursed (or perhaps blessed) with a great deal of morning-after nausea. Never once in my life have I had a headache, which fact leads me to believe that I was an alcoholic almost from the start. My whole life seemed to be centered around doing what I wanted to do, without regard for the rights, wishes, or privileges of anyone else; a state of mind which became more and more predominant as the years passed. I was graduated “summa cum laude” in the eyes of the drinking fraternity, but not in the eyes of the Dean.”
We see that Dr. Bob was not fond of church and was able to keep a commitment for 40 years.
He had an idea that his real problem was selfishness; he attributes his alcoholism to being selfish.

Dr. Bob attended Dartmouth College, “one of the best colleges in the country” where his drinking progressed. He had “lots of fun and not much grief.” His whole life seemed to be centered on pleasing himself, a condition which grew with time.
Selfish and self centered - ring any Bells?

“The next three years I spent in Boston, Chicago, and Montreal in the employ of a large manufacturing concern, selling railway supplies, gas engines of all sorts, and many other items of heavy hardware. During these years, I drank as much as my purse permitted, still without paying too great a penalty, although I was beginning to have morning jitters at times. I lost only a half day’s work during these three years.
My next move was to take up the study of medicine, entering one of the largest universities in the country. There I took up the business of drinking with much greater earnestness than I had previously shown. On account of my enormous capacity for beer, I was elected to membership in one of the drinking societies, and soon became one of the leading spirits. Many mornings I have gone to classes, and even though fully prepared, would turn and walk back to the fraternity house because of my jitters, not daring to enter the classroom for fear of making a scene should I be called on for recitation.
This went from bad to worse until Sophomore spring when, after a prolonged period of drinking, I made up my mind that I could not complete my course, so I packed my grip and went South to spend a month on a large farm owned by a friend of mine. When I got the fog out of my brain, I decided that quitting school was very foolish and that I had better return and continue my work. When I reached school, I discovered the faculty had other ideas on the subject. After much argument they allowed me to return and take my exams, all of which I passed creditably. But they were much disgusted and told me they would attempt to struggle along without my presence. After many painful discussions, they finally gave me my credits and I migrated to another of the leading universities of the country and entered as a Junior that fall.”
“entering one of the largest universities in the country” - University of Michigan
“I migrated to another of the leading universities of the” - Rush Medical University
Dr Bobs drinking progressed, he began to get the shakes in the morning, he couldn’t attend classes because of them and eventually left school after a “prolonged period of drinking”.
Does anyone know what large company Dr. Bob worked for selling railway supplies, gas engines and heavy hardware?

“There my drinking became so much worse that the boys in the fraternity house where I lived felt forced to send for my father, who made a long journey in the vain endeavor to get me straightened around. This had little effect however for I kept on drinking and used a great deal more hard liquor than in former years.
Coming up to final exams I went on a particularly strenuous spree. When I went in to write the examinations, my hand trembled so I could not hold a pencil. I passed in at least three absolutely blank books. I was, of course, soon on the carpet and the upshot was that I had to go back for two more quarters and remain absolutely dry, if I wished to graduate. This I did, and proved myself satisfactory to the faculty, both in deportment and scholastically.
I conducted myself so creditably that I was able to secure a much coveted internship in a western city, where I spent two years. During these two years I was kept so busy that I hardly left the hospital at all. Consequently, I could not get into any trouble. When those two years were up, I opened an office downtown. I had some money, all the time in the world, and considerable stomach trouble. I soon discovered that a couple of drinks would alleviate my gastric distress, at least for a few hours at a time, so it was not at all difficult for me to return to my former excessive indulgence.
By this time I was beginning to pay very dearly physically and, in hope of relief, voluntarily incarcerated myself at least a dozen times in one of the local sanitariums.”
Dr. Bobs drinking begins to have an effect on his family, typically our families try over and over to help us; we give them hope and disappointment again and again.

Dr. Bob was able to stop drinking for a period of time (probably about 20 weeks, which would be two quarters). Stopping is sometimes possible, it’s stopping completely and the control part that we can’t master. Eventually Dr. Bob turns to voluntary incarceration to attempt to get “relief”.
Akron Ohio – “internship in a western city”
Fair Oaks Villa, Cuyahoga Falls, Ohio - “one of the local sanitariums.”

“I was between Scylla and Charybdis now, because if I did not drink my stomach tortured me, and if I did, my nerves did the same thing. After three years of this, I wound up in the local hospital where they attempted to help me, but I would get my friends to smuggle me a quart, or I would steal the alcohol about the building, so that I got rapidly worse.
Finally my father had to send a doctor out from my home town who managed to get me back there in some way, and I was in bed about two months before I could venture out of the house. I stayed about town a couple of months more and then returned to resume my practice. I think I must have been thoroughly scared by what had happened, or by the doctor, or probably both, so that I did not touch a drink again until the country went dry.
With the passing of the Eighteenth Amendment I felt quite safe. I knew everyone would buy a few bottles, or cases, of liquor as their exchequers permitted, and that it would soon be gone. Therefore it would make no great difference, even if I should do some drinking. At that time I was not aware of the almost unlimited supply the government made it possible for us doctors to obtain, neither had I any knowledge of the bootlegger who soon appeared on the horizon. I drank with moderation at first, but it took me only a relatively short time to drift back into the old habits which had wound up so disastrously before.
During the next few years, I developed two distinct phobias. One was the fear of not sleeping, and the other was the fear of running out of liquor.”
“Scylla and Charybdis” is from The Odyssey written between 7 and 8 BC, it predates our “between a rock and a hard place”

Dr. Bob can no longer function with or without alcohol and ends up in the Peoples Hospital in Akron, his father sends a doctor from St. Johnsbury, Vermont, Dr. Bobs hometown. This was in 1914 the Eighteenth Amendment became effective on January 16, 1920 - so once again Dr. Bob is determined to stop drinking and is able to stay away for long period of time, but as soon as he “drank with moderation” in a relatively short time it turned disastrous. Does this sound familiar, “fear of not sleeping, and … fear of running out of liquor.”?
I would like to hear from any of you history buffs concerning Dr. Bob. There is plenty written about Bills early days but our history concerning Dr. Bob, before he met Bill, seems to be sparse.

“Not being a man of means, I knew that if I did not stay sober enough to earn money, I would run out of liquor. Most of the time, therefore, I did not take the morning drink which I craved so badly, but instead would fill up on large doses of sedatives to quiet the jitters, which distressed me terribly. Occasionally, I would yield to the morning craving, but if I did, it would be only a few hours before I would be quite unfit for work. This would lessen my chances of smuggling some home that evening, which in turn would mean a night of futile tossing around in bed followed by a morning of unbearable jitters. During the subsequent fifteen years I had sense enough never to go to the hospital if I had been drinking, and very seldom did I receive patients. I would sometimes hide out in one of the clubs of which I was a member, and had the habit at times of registering at a hotel under a fictitious name. But my friends usually found me and I would go home if they promised that I should not be scolded.
If my wife was planning to go out in the afternoon, I would get a large supply of liquor and smuggle it home and hide it in the coal bin, the clothes chute, over door jambs, over beams in the cellar and in cracks in the cellar tile. I also made use of old trunks and chests, the old can container, and even the ash container. The water tank on the toilet I never used, because that looked too easy. I found out later that my wife inspected it frequently. I used to put eight or twelve ounce bottles of alcohol in a fur lined glove and toss it onto the back airing porch when winter days got dark enough. My bootlegger had hidden alcohol at the back steps where I could get it at my convenience.”

As his alcoholism progressed Dr. Bob tried - staying sober to earn money for liquor, fighting the morning drink, taking sedatives to quiet his nerves, drinking in the morning, smuggling booze home, spent nights of tossing in bed, morning jitters, didn’t go certain places when drinking, hiding out, registering under a false name, hiding from friends and family, hiding liquor and having bootleggers drop booze off for him. I can relate to Dr. Bob

“Sometimes I would bring it in my pockets, but they were inspected, and that became too risky. I used also to put it up in four ounce bottles and stick several in my stocking tops. This worked nicely until my wife and I went to see Wallace Beery in “Tugboat Annie,” after which the pant-leg and stocking racket were out!
I will not take space to relate all my hospital or sanitarium experiences.
During all this time we became more or less ostracized by our friends. We could not be invited out because I would surely get tight and my wife dared not invite people in for the same reason. My phobia for sleeplessness demanded that I get drunk every night, but in order to get more liquor for the next night, I had to stay sober during the day, at least up to four o’clock. This routine went on with few interruptions for seventeen years. It was really a horrible nightmare, this earning money, getting liquor, smuggling it home, getting drunk, morning jitters, taking large doses of sedatives to make it possible for me to earn more money, and so on ad nauseam. I used to promise my wife, my friends, and my children that I would drink no more— promises which seldom kept me sober even through the day, though I was very sincere when I made them.
For the benefit of those experimentally inclined, I should mention the so-called beer experiment. When beer first came back, I thought that I was safe. I could drink all I wanted of that. It was harmless; nobody ever got drunk on beer. So I filled the cellar full, with the permission of my good wife. It was not long before I was drinking at least a case and a half a day.”

So here is Dr. Bob - ostracized by friends, can’t socialize because he would get drunk, can’t sleep without getting drunk, 17 years of torment for his family. Sincere promises, bad experiences, love or fear can’t keep an alcoholic sober, we don’t have the power. And even after learning that, even after it makes sense, after it is confirmed in our experience, we still try to stop drinking by our so called will power. God Blessed us all. Welcome, my name is mike and I am " experimentally inclined" but today, thank God, I am experimenting with a new way of life and thankfully I had nothing to do with the plan.

“I put on thirty pounds of weight in about two months, looked like a pig, and was uncomfortable from shortness of breath. It then occurred to me that after one was all smelled up with beer nobody could tell what had been drunk, so I began to fortify my beer with straight alcohol. Of course, the result was very bad, and that ended the beer experiment.
About the time of the beer experiment I was thrown in with a crowd of people who attracted me because of their seeming poise, health, and happiness. They spoke with great freedom from embarrassment, which I could never do, and they seemed very much at ease on all occasions and appeared very healthy. More than these attributes, they seemed to be happy. I was self conscious and ill at ease most of the time, my health was at the breaking point, and I was thoroughly miserable. I sensed they had something I did not have, from which I might readily profit. I learned that it was something of a spiritual nature, which did not appeal to me very much, but I thought it could do no harm. I gave the matter much time and study for the next two and a half years, but still got tight every night nevertheless. I read everything I could find, and talked to everyone who I thought knew anything about it.
My wife became deeply interested and it was her interest that sustained mine, though I at no time sensed that it might be an answer to my liquor problem. How my wife kept her faith and courage during all those years, I’ll never know, but she did. If she had not, I know I would have been dead a long time ago. For some reason, we alcoholics seem to have the gift of picking out the world’s finest women.”
That’s crystal clear alcoholic thinking - fortify beer with straight alcohol, who will know?

I can relate to Dr. Bob “. I was self conscious and ill at ease most of the time” yet I wanted to be like these folks - “poise, health, and happiness. They spoke with great freedom from embarrassment, which I could never do, and they seemed very much at ease on all occasions and appeared very healthy”

“thrown in with a crowd of people” Dr. Bob meets the Oxford Group, thanks to his wife Anne Smith, she had been attending the OG for about 2 years before Dr. Bob went. Probably how Anne dealt with the pain of living with an alcoholic, many of our loved ones turn to the one thing that works – prayer and dependence upon God.
Here is a nice article on “the mother of AA” http://silkworth.net/dickb/smith01.html

Dr. Bob “gave the [OG & prayer] much time and study for the next two and a half years, but still got tight every night nevertheless. I read everything I could find, and talked to everyone who I thought knew anything about it.”
So what changed? Dr. Bob had been living in and around the solution. Why wasn’t he saved? What did Bill bring to Bob that made a difference?
Do you think we “have the gift of picking out the world’s finest women”? or is that God’s way of protecting us? Clearly not every alcoholic is blessed with a friend with “faith and courage”?
“Why they should be subjected to the tortures we inflict upon them, I cannot explain.

About this time a lady called up my wife one Saturday afternoon, saying she wanted me to come over that evening to meet a friend of hers who might help me. It was the day before Mother’s Day and I had come home plastered, carrying a big potted plant which I set down on the table and forthwith went upstairs and passed out. The next day she called again. Wishing to be polite, though I felt very badly, I said, “Let’s make the call,” and extracted from my wife a promise that we would not stay over fifteen minutes.

We entered her house at exactly five o’clock and it was eleven fifteen when we left. I had a couple of shorter talks with this man afterward, and stopped drinking abruptly. This dry spell lasted for about three weeks; then I went to Atlantic City to attend several days’ meeting of a national society of which I was a member. I drank all the scotch they had on the train and bought several quarts on my way to the hotel. This was on Sunday. I got tight that night, stayed sober Monday till after the dinner and then proceeded to get tight again. I drank all I dared in the bar, and then went to my room to finish the job. Tuesday I started in the morning, getting well organized by noon. I did not want to disgrace myself so I then checked out. I bought some more liquor on the way to the depot. I had to wait some time for the train. I remember nothing from then on until I woke up at a friend’s house, in a town near home. These good people notified my wife, who sent my newly made friend over to get me.”
That first question is easy enough to answer, they shouldn’t be.

The lady that called Anne Smith was Henrietta Seiberling, she and her OG group had been praying for Dr. Bob, to no avail. When Bill was alone and afraid at the mayflower hotel he reached out and was eventually put in contact with Henrietta. See pages 154-155
Bills experience and information caught Dr. Bob’s attention, and he gained another valuable piece of the puzzle through relapse. Knowledge of the problem and the solution is not enough.

I pray that what I have been given doesn’t keep me from working these steps with sincerity and enthusiasm. Prayer, mediation and being of service to others is all that has ever helped me. I pray for the grace to stay in the solution.

“He came and got me home and to bed, gave me a few drinks that night, and one bottle of beer the next morning.
That was June 10, 1935, and that was my last drink. As I write nearly four years have passed.
The question which might naturally come into your mind would be: “What did the man do or say that was different from what others had done or said?” It must be remembered that I had read a great deal and talked to everyone who knew, or thought they knew anything about the subject of alcoholism. But this was a man who had experienced many years of frightful drinking, who had had most all the drunkard’s experiences known to man, but who had been cured by the very means I had been trying to employ, that is to say the spiritual approach. He gave me information about the subject of alcoholism which was undoubtedly helpful. Of far more importance was the fact that he was the first living human with whom I had ever talked, who knew what he was talking about in regard to alcoholism from actual experience. In other words, he talked my language. He knew all the answers, and certainly not because he had picked them up in his reading.
It is a most wonderful blessing to be relieved of the terrible curse with which I was afflicted. My health is good and I have regained my self-respect and the respect of my colleagues. My home life is ideal and my business is as good as can be expected in these uncertain times.”
Do I know what I am talking about in and around alcoholism?
Can I offer a concise, understandable explanation of our illness?
Can I clearly explain what I used to be like, what happened, what I do and what I am like now?
Can I offer clear suggestions for following our program?
Am I willing to go to any lengths to pass on this “wonderful blessing”?

“I spend a great deal of time passing on what I learned to others who want and need it badly. I do it for four reasons:
1. Sense of duty.
2. It is a pleasure.
3. Because in so doing I am paying my debt to the man who took time to pass it on to me.
4. Because every time I do it I take out a little more insurance for myself against a possible slip.
Unlike most of our crowd, I did not get over my craving for liquor much during the first two and one-half years of abstinence. It was almost always with me. But at no time have I been anywhere near yielding. I used to get terribly upset when I saw my friends drink and knew I could not, but I schooled myself to believe that though I once had the same privilege, I had abused it so frightfully that it was withdrawn. So it doesn’t behoove me to squawk about it for, after all, nobody ever had to throw me down and pour liquor down my throat.
If you think you are an atheist, an agnostic, a skeptic, or have any other form of intellectual pride which keeps you from accepting what is in this book, I feel sorry for you. If you still think you are strong enough to beat the game alone, that is your affair. But if you really and truly want to quit drinking liquor for good and all, and sincerely feel that you must have some help, we know that we have an answer for you. It never fails, if you go about it with one half the zeal you have been in the habit of showing when you were getting another drink.
Your Heavenly Father will never let you down!
Do I “spend a great deal of time passing on what I learned to others who want and need it badly”?
Do I have a sense of duty? Do I take pleasure in helping others? Am I paying my thanks to the men and women who took and still take the time to carry our message?
Do I have “intellectual pride”? Do I know so much that I can’t see something new?
Have I accepted what is in this book? If I have am I working at it?

Dr. Bob was known as the “Prince of the twelve steppers” he helped 5000 alcoholics during his 15 years of working our program, his humility and work with others legendary and embodies the core of our program.

That last question is important for me, there are traps here, I am in constant danger of getting comfortable. Thinking and talking about AA is not AA, thinking and talking prayer, meditation, fellowshipping and helping others is. On a daily basis

readings.title: About This Study · How to Use It

items.x: Thank you all for joining this group; if you have never posted please consider introducing yourself or send me your name so I can introduce you to our group, either way, thank you.
Each day we send out a quote from our basic text. If you have experience with it or a question please share. We are all looking for a new experience with this work and could use a fresh perspective.

Most of what I post was shown to me by a woman named Fran Tenser who was a recovered member of alcoholics anonymous, God bless her; she was a kind and giving soul; I am here, free happy and sober in large part to her service and love.
The basic format calls for us to:
Stop at each period. If the sentence has directions, follow them. If the sentence is a statement, turn it into a question and ask myself if that is or was me. i.e..
"We, OF Alcoholics Anonymous, are more than one hundred men and women who have recovered from a seemingly hopeless state of mind and body."
Am I hopeless of mind (do I still obsess - do I have the ability to believe a lie, do I suffer from strange mental blank spots)
Am I hopeless of body (when I start can I control the amount I take - or do I suffer from the allergy - the phenomenon of craving)
Do I believe that I can recover? Do I want to recover? Am I willing to do what I am told to do to recover?

These questions can help to place me. Is it or was it true for me? I use the question as a meditation, waiting for the answer to come to me, not from me. My very best thinking got me here; my very best thinking got me to pick up a drink over and over even though I knew that it was destructive, even after I had promised myself I would never do this again. So before I start I say a simple prayer asking my Creator take from me what I think I know, open my heart and mind and allow me to see the truth.
Fran also taught me to personalize my book - when reading I change: us to me, we - I, our - my.

Please join in and share your experience and what you see that we might miss. I ask that we stay on topic as best we can, but please share what you question, feel and have. Hopefully this will be used as an action based study; and we will do what we are talking about.
If you ever have experience, questions or ideas please share them, you may be helping more than you may know.
We will begin with the title page tomorrow, although I like to look to the first page in our book to remind myself that it contains all I really know about everything I think I know.
Further reading Mike shared
http://www.barefootsworld.net/aa-bbtrivia.html
http://silkworth.net/aahistory/timelines_historic_aa_events.html

readings.title: The Purpose of the Big Book

items.x: The main purpose of the “Big Book” (Alcoholics Anonymous) is to show other alcoholics precisely how the first members recovered from a seemingly hopeless state of mind and body.
From the Foreword to the First Edition
“To show other alcoholics PRECISELY HOW WE HAVE RECOVERED is the main purpose of this book.”
The circle and the triangle represent our 3-fold disease and our 3-fold program of action. When I am engaged in all of three parts of our three fold solution I cannot drink even if I would. Page 57

God, please set aside everything I think
I know about myself, my disease, the 12 Steps
and You, for an open mind and a new
experience of myself, my disease, the 12 Steps
and especially You!
Please help me to see the truth.
Where this prayer comes from
The prayer is based on several concepts referenced in the Big Book.
Pg 42, paragraph 2:
“It meant I would have to throw several lifelong conceptions out of the window”
Page 46, paragraph 1:

“We found that as soon as we were able to lay aside prejudice and express even a willingness to believe in a power greater than ourselves. We commenced to get results even though it was impossible for any of us fully define or comprehend that power which is God.”
Pg 47, paragraph 4:
“Do not let any prejudice you may have against any spiritual terms deter you from honestly asking yourself what they mean to you.”
Pg 47, paragraph 4:
“Besides a seeming inability to accept much on faith, we often found ourselves handicapped by obstinacy, sensitiveness, and unreasoning prejudice.”
“It finally beat us into a state of reasonableness. Sometimes this was a tedious process; we hope no one else will be prejudiced for as long as some of us were.”
Page 49, paragraph 2:
“We who have traveled this dubious path, beg you to lay aside prejudice, even against organized religion.”
Page 58, paragraph 3:
“Some of us have tried to hold on to our old ideas and the result was nil until we let go absolutely.”

Dear God, I humbly offer myself to you, to do with me as you will. I place myself unreservedly under Your care and Your direction. I admit for the first time that of myself I am nothing; that without You I am lost. Please stay with me and guide me throughout this day.
Amen

God, I offer myself to Thee-to build with me and to do with me as Thou wilt. Relieve me of the bondage of self, that I may better do Thy will. Take away my difficulties, that victory over them may bear witness to those I would help of Thy Power, Thy Love, and Thy Way of life. May I do Thy will always!

My Creator, I am now willing that you should have all of me, good and bad. I pray that you now remove from me every single defect of character which stands in the way of my usefulness to you and my fellows. Grant me strength, as I go out from here, to do your bidding. Amen.
Mike: “Do the seventh step prayer every morning and night with the third step prayer on your knees.”

God, please help me show (name) the same tolerance, pity, and patience I would cheerfully grant a sick friend. Dear God, please show me how can I be helpful to (name) and save me from being angry. Thy will, not mine be done, Amen.
In the daily post this prayer uses the example name “Denny”; here it reads “(name)” so you can say it for anyone.
Dear God please demonstrate through me what you can do. Please remove my fear and direct my attention to what You would have me be.

God, please help me to mold my ideals and live up to them. Please show me what to do in each of these matters. I believe in your guidance and that you, as the final judge can bring me the sanity and strength I need to do the right thing and to take me to a better place. Amen
Dear God please give me strength and direction to do the right thing. Allow me a helpful and forgiving spirit. Help me to be humble, calm, frank, and open and to stick to my faults. Amen
Dear God, please remove my selfishness, dishonesty, resentment, and fear and show me the way to Love and tolerance of others.
My Creator, please help me watch for selfishness, dishonesty, resentment, and fear. And when they crop up, please give me a prayer.
Please take this from me, I don’t want to be like this anymore. Amen.
Dear God please give me love and tolerance of others. Please make me a channel of your peace…
On awakening
Dear God, please direct my thinking; divorce me from self-pity, dishonest and self-seeking motives.
Closing prayer after meditation
My Creator please show me all through the day what my next step is to be, please grant me freedom from self, Thy will be done. Amen.
Throughout the day
Thy will be done.
Page 89
intensive work with other alcoholics.
Don't start out as an evangelist or reformer.
So cooperate; never criticize. To be helpful is our only aim.
Page 90
find out all you can about him.
If he does not want to stop drinking, don't waste time trying to persuade him.
This advice is given for his family also.
Sometimes it is wise to wait till he goes on a binge.
Wait for the end of the spree, or at least for a lucid interval.
ask him if he wants to quit for good and if he would go to any extreme to do so.
then his attention should be drawn to you as a person who has recovered.
You should be described to him as one of a fellowship who, as part of their own recovery, try to help others and who will be glad to talk to him if he cares to see you.
Page 91
Make sure he understands he is under no pressure
Call on him while he is still jittery. He may be more receptive when depressed.
See your man alone
Tell him enough about your drinking habits, symptoms, and experiences to encourage him to speak of himself.
Let him talk, learn how to best approach him
If he is in a serious mood dwell on the troubles liquor has caused you
be careful not to moralize or lecture.
through your story, show him that you know all about drinking.
Page 92
Tell him how baffled you were, how you finally learned that you were sick. Give him an account of the struggles you made to stop.
Show him the mental twist which leads to the first drink - do this as it is done it in the chapter on alcoholism.
If you are satisfied that he is a real alcoholic, begin to dwell on the hopeless feature of the malady.
Show him, from your own experience, how the queer mental condition surrounding that first drink prevents normal functioning of the will power
Don't, at this stage, refer to this book, unless he has seen it and wishes to discuss it. (Hold off on the solution - make sure he is tired and desperate)
Don’t brand him as an alcoholic. Let him draw his own conclusion.
If he sticks to the idea that he can still control his drinking, tell him that possibly he can. (plant the seed)
Insist that if he is severely afflicted, there may be little chance he can recover by himself.
speak of alcoholism as an illness, a fatal malady. Talk about the conditions of body and mind.
Explain that many are doomed and never realize it.
talk to him about the hopelessness of alcoholism because you offer a solution. talk to him about the hopelessness of alcoholism because you offer a solution.
Page 93
Let him ask you how you got well, if he will.
Tell him exactly what happened to you.

Stress the spiritual feature freely. If the man be agnostic or atheist, make it emphatic that he does not have to agree with your conception of God. He can choose any conception he likes, provided it makes sense to him.
The main thing is that he be willing to believe in a Power greater than himself and that he live by spiritual principles.
use everyday language to describe spiritual principles.
Don't arousing any prejudice, no matter what your own convictions are.
Let him see that you are not there to instruct him in religion.
Admit that he probably knows more about it than you do, but call to his attention the fact that however deep his faith and knowledge, he could not have applied it or he would not drink.
Page 94

Outline the program of action, explaining how you made a self-appraisal, how you straightened out your past and why you are now endeavoring to be helpful to him. It is important for him to realize that your attempt to pass this on to him plays a vital part in your own recovery.
Make it plain he is under no obligation to you, that you hope only that he will try to help other alcoholics when he escapes his own difficulties.
Suggest how important it is that he place the welfare of other people ahead of his own.
Make it clear that he is not under pressure, that he needn't see you again if he doesn't want to.
Your talk should be sane, quiet and full of human understanding, you should be a friend.
The more hopeless he feels, the better. He will be more likely to follow our suggestions.
If he/she gives reasons why they need not follow all of the program. Tell them you once felt as they do, but you doubt you would have made much progress had you not been thorough.
tell him about the Fellowship of Alcoholics Anonymous. If he shows interest, lend him your copy of this book.
Page 95
Do not wear out your welcome. Give him a chance to think it over.
If he is anxious to proceed at once this is sometimes a mistake. Do not rush the prospect.
You will be most successful with alcoholics if you do not exhibit any passion for crusade or reform.
Never talk down to an alcoholic from any moral or spiritual hilltop; simply lay out the kit of spiritual tools for his inspection.
Show him how they worked with you.
Offer him friendship and fellowship. Tell him that if he wants to get well you will do anything to help.

If he is not interested in your solution, if he expects you to act only as a banker for his financial difficulties or a nurse for his sprees, you may have to drop him until he changes his mind. This he may do after he gets hurt some more.
If he is sincerely interested and wants to see you again, ask him to read this book in the interval.
After doing that, he must decide for himself whether he wants to go on. If he wants to
Do not push or prod the newcomer.
If he is to find God, the desire must come from within.

If he thinks he can do the job in some other way, or prefers some other spiritual approach, encourage him to follow his own conscience. Point out that we have an approach that worked for us and millions of others and that you would like, in any case, to stay in a position to be helpful should booze change their mind.
Page 96
find someone desperate enough to accept with eagerness what you offer
so each day I claim spiritual progress in the simple way our book outlines on pages 84 – 86 I work step ten, eleven and twelve daily, I help others as best I can and pass it on.

I see two ways to my first step at a depth sufficient for me to work the program as if my life depended upon it. 1 is through working the steps 2. Is after I have had enough ego deflation to see that working the steps is my only hope the realize that my way does not and will not ever work

for me it was not about where I ended up or what happened to me, what I found in a prison cell was my powerlessness, our book says it best I couldn't postpone or evade it. All my skills, my thinking, all my power, my work, my intelligence, cleverness and great ideas was a prison cell. Me, as I highly as I thought of myself I couldn't evade the reality that on my own no matter what the circumstance the very best I could do was end up incarcerated,

I had worked in prisons long enough to see that once a man gets stuck in the system it is almost inevitable he will remain in the system. my plan, the very best I could come up with, involved suicide, if all else failed, I could kill myself. I had been trying to change my life long enough to realize that I couldn't. but I could end it. that was always there, my backup plan was to put an end to this miserable existence once and for all, if all else failed (again) I could end it.
alcoholics share 2 things in common, once we start drinking we cannot stop and when we vow to stop we cannot stay stopped. the third is loneliness and heartache.
I am part of a fellowship of men and women that helps others to recover from alcoholism.

I am not allied with any sect, denomination, politics, organization or institutions I do not wish to engage in any controversy, I neither endorse nor oppose any causes. my primary purpose is to help other alcoholics to achieve sobriety.
I know better but at any given time I want to engage in controversy, but thankfully today I am not going to. Peace and love.

steps.name: Powerless and unmanageable
steps.wording: We admitted we were powerless over alcohol—that our lives had become unmanageable.

items.x: We admitted we were powerless over alcohol—that our lives had become unmanageable.
Big Book, page 59
In short
Read pages 35–43 Jim, the jaywalker and Fred. Personalize these examples.

Step One has two parts. “Powerless” means we have lost choice (we said we would quit, we can't and we drink again) and lost control (we said we would only have a couple and we can't control the amount we drink once we start). An “unmanageable life” is a life that is crazy not happy, joyous and free, whether we are drunk or dry. We seem to have an itch we just can't scratch.

Alcoholism is a two-fold illness: an allergy of the body (once we start, the phenomenon of craving takes over) and an obsession of the mind, which the Big Book calls the main problem. Every drunk began from a state of sobriety: we have a body that can’t take it and a mind that can’t leave it alone.
What to do
Answer one simple question from your own experience: once you started drinking, did you lose control over the amount you drank?
Look at your sober thinking: did you have a mental defense against the first drink that worked every time?

How many times did you pick up a drink without any thought, or with a thought that sounded like common sense, and only after the first drink did you realize that you've done it again? Now you can't stop, so you go ahead and say, "I'll start again tomorrow." For me, I was crazy before the drink, when 100% sober; only after drinking was my sanity restored and I realized I'd done it again.
Alcohol restores my sanity, but I can no longer take its effect. I must replace it with something else. That something else is the program of Alcoholics Anonymous.
Concede to your innermost self that you are a real alcoholic—not a moderate or hard drinker.
Ask yourself
Did I ever say I would quit, try to quit, and not quit? (Lost choice.)
Did I ever plan to control the amount I drank and fail? (Lost control.)
Have I ever “suddenly thought it would be OK to take a drink,” in a strange mental blank spot, after all I knew?
Do I concede that I am physically and mentally powerless over alcohol?
Read in the Big Book
Chapter 2, There Is a Solution (pages 17–29)
Pages 30 and 45
Page 23: the main problem centers in the mind
Sources: A Guide for Working the Steps with Alcoholics (main); questions on the mental blank spot and the first drink from steps_1-12; Study Guide to the AA Big Book (reading pages).

steps.name: Came to believe
steps.wording: Came to believe that a Power greater than ourselves could restore us to sanity.

items.x: Came to believe that a Power greater than ourselves could restore us to sanity.
Big Book, page 59
In short
This is about you and your need for power – “came to believe”

Step 2 doesn't say you have to believe, it says came to believe. The only question you have to ask yourself is: is it **possible** that there is something more powerful than me? I already know that alcohol is more powerful than me; now, is there something more powerful than me that can help me?
Read pages 44–57 (the entire chapter).
Continue to turn statements to questions, mark them in your book and consider them.

When you are familiar with the chapter and the questions you have marked in your book and considered, look at the first half of Step 2, page 47: “Do I now believe, or am I even willing to believe, that there is a Power greater than myself?” If this is not your first time, add this to the consideration: [that can take me beyond where I am?] To make this consideration, look through the entire chapter and mark in color words or statements that help you see where you don’t believe, i.e. “honest doubt”, “prejudice”, “skepticism”, “sensitiveness”, etc. After marking them, consider in prayer each word or statement that was marked to honestly admit, or at least consider, your current agnosticism.
Referring back to the question “a power that can take me beyond where I am,” consider using page 52 as a guide. Look at this question in relation to each area of your life.
Review in prayer all marked considerations and answer the question “Do I now believe, or am I even willing to believe, that there is a Power greater than myself?”

To consider the second half of Step 2, the second step choice or proposition, page 53: “either God is everything or else He is nothing. God either is, or He isn't.” To make that consideration, look through the entire chapter and mark in color everything you can find that “takes you from willingness to believe – to choosing God as being everything or nothing.” Mark these considerations in a prayerful way.
Using page 52 as a guide, look at each area of your life; consider, based on all you’ve seen with the first and second step, “what if God is nothing?”
Then, doing the entire prayerful review again, consider: what if God is everything?
Now make a choice.
What to do
Be honest: list some self-destructive things you have done, drunk and dry.
Notice the two kinds of thoughts you have had: self-destructive ones, and the creative ones that sometimes made you walk away from harm.
Become willing to believe in a Power greater than yourself; you are free to form your own concept of it.
Ask yourself
Is it possible that I am being held back by “honest doubt”, “prejudice”, “skepticism”, “sensitiveness”, fear? Add to this list freely.
Do I now believe, or am I even willing to believe, that it is possible there is a Power greater than myself?
Is it possible that the people that wrote this book and those that I hear speak are telling me the truth, that there is a power that can take me beyond where I am?
Does this make sense, that “either God is everything or else He is nothing. God either is, or He isn't.”?
Read in the Big Book
Chapter 4, We Agnostics, pages 44–57 (the entire chapter)
Sources: A Guide for Working the Steps with Alcoholics (main); Study Guide to the AA Big Book (reading pages).

steps.name: Made a decision
steps.wording: Made a decision to turn our will and our lives over to the care of God as we understood Him.

items.x: Made a decision to turn our will and our lives over to the care of God as we understood Him.
Big Book, page 59
In short

Step Three is a decision. The guide reads it with the understood words put back: we made a decision to turn our self-will and our unmanageable lives over to the care of a Higher Power. Any name or idea of that Power will do; the Big Book says agnostics are no obstacle, and AA is spiritual, not religious.

The guide says that in taking this step you admit three things: you have tried to manage alone and it isn’t working; you are turning the unmanageable part of your life over to a new manager; and you decide to do Steps 4 through 12, because they are what get us out of self-will. Those who go back out most often stop at Step Three.
Read from page 58 to the bottom of page 63.
Continue to turn statements to questions, mark them in your book and consider them.
Consider the first paragraph on page 58 (see the questions below).
Consider all of paragraph 2 on page 60, the A, B, C’s. Do a prayerful review of all consideration questions from The Doctor’s Opinion to the A, B, C’s.

Consider the first requirement of the Third Step, page 60 paragraph 4 through page 62 (not including the last paragraph). To consider this requirement, read the statements in the first person, i.e. the first requirement is that “I am convinced that my life run on my will, will never be (has never been) a success.”
Being convinced of this requirement (my life run on my will, will never be a success), consider what this Third Step decision means to you, page 60 bottom paragraph:

Having considered these terms and what they mean to you, get quiet and make a decision that from here after in this drama of life, God is going to be my Director. He is the Principal; I am His agent. He is the Father, and I am His child.
Affirm your decision with our Third Step Prayer on page 63.
What to do
Compare the two voices: the Higher Power says “harm no one, be humble, be still, serve all,” while the ego says “feel important, control everyone, use all, go-do-zoom.”
See that self-will and ego (a liar that protects the false self-image) were driving the insane behavior.
Make the decision, and confirm it by saying the Third Step affirmation below.
Ask yourself
Is this me? (page 58, first paragraph)
Have I decided I want what they have?
Am I willing to go to any length to get it?
Am I willing to take certain steps?
Am I convinced of these three pertinent ideas? (page 60, the A, B, C’s)
Read in the Big Book
How It Works, pages 58–63 (to the bottom of page 63)
Sources: A Guide for Working the Steps with Alcoholics (main); Study Guide to the AA Big Book (reading pages).

steps.name: Moral inventory
steps.wording: Made a searching and fearless moral inventory of ourselves.

items.x: Made a searching and fearless moral inventory of ourselves.
Big Book, page 59
In short

Like a failing business, we take an inventory of assets and liabilities to see what has been causing the trouble. We are looking for the nature of our wrongs, not every wrong, so the writing is quick and to the point: the Big Book’s example on page 65 is as detailed as it needs to be.

What we criticize in others is often what we dislike in ourselves (“if you spot it, you got it”), so resentments become a mirror. The inventory covers resentments, fears and sex conduct, and is meant to reveal the self-will behind them.
What to do
Column 1: list 4 or more people, institutions or rules you resent.
Column 2: write about three words for what is wrong with each (for example: gossip, unreasonable, controlling).
Column 3: how each one affected your pride, self-esteem, ambitions, emotional and financial security, sex relations and personal relations.
Column 4: in each case, where were you selfish, self-seeking, dishonest or afraid? Ask where you have been those same things you wrote about others.
Fears: look for the three sponsoring thoughts: I am not enough, I will never have enough, and so I will be abandoned.
Sex conduct: for each relationship, where were you selfish, dishonest or inconsiderate, and where did you arouse jealousy, suspicion or bitterness? What should you have done instead?
Ask yourself
Where have I tried to have a person meet needs that only the Higher Power can meet?
Where, in each case, was my own behavior insane: selfish, dishonest, self-seeking or afraid?
Read in the Big Book
How It Works, pages 64–67 (resentment)
Pages 67–68 (fear)
Pages 68–71 (sex conduct, to the end of Chapter 5)
Sources: A Guide for Working the Steps with Alcoholics (main); fear and sex-inventory points from A Twelve-Step Journey to Self-Transformation; Study Guide to the AA Big Book (reading pages).

steps.name: Admitted the exact nature
steps.wording: Admitted to God, to ourselves, and to another human being the exact nature of our wrongs.

items.x: Admitted to God, to ourselves, and to another human being the exact nature of our wrongs.
Big Book, page 59
In short

In the guide, Steps 4 and 5 are done together in one session: you read your columns aloud to the person taking you through, who helps you see your part. The aim is the exact nature of the wrongs (the defects behind them), not a list of every wrong.
The Twelve-Step Journey calls Step Five a life-and-death matter: it is the death of the self-will persona and the start of a new life.
What to do
Choose someone who has done the work, and go over your inventory together without holding back.
For each resentment, name your part plainly.
Notice that your own judgments of others reflected the very faults you found in yourself.
Look for anything you have done to people that needs forgiving.
Ask yourself
Have I told the whole truth to God, to myself and to another person?
Can I see the defects, not just the events, that caused my troubles?
Read in the Big Book
Chapter 6, Into Action, pages 72–75 (to “…they will be honored by our confidence”)
Page 75 (“We pocket our pride…” to “…mortar without sand?”)
Sources: A Guide for Working the Steps with Alcoholics (main); A Twelve-Step Journey to Self-Transformation; Study Guide to the AA Big Book (reading pages).

steps.name: Entirely ready
steps.wording: Were entirely ready to have God remove all these defects of character.

items.x: Were entirely ready to have God remove all these defects of character.
Big Book, page 59
In short

Having seen the defects that drove our wrongs, we become willing to let them go. The guide asks: since these defects made life unmanageable and insane, don’t you want to be rid of them, and are you willing to ask for sane guidance instead?

The Journey adds a review on returning home: have I had a solid experience with the first five steps, and do I truly believe the Power will remove these defects? If they stay, they lead back to the spiritual malady, and to a drink.
What to do
Spend an hour at home reviewing what you have learned, as the Big Book suggests.
Use the guide’s list of 20 assets and liabilities (forgiveness or resentment, honesty or lying, patience or impatience, and so on) and circle the liabilities that have been part of your life.
Write out the behaviors and beliefs that came from self-will and see the effect they had on you and those around you.
If you aren’t yet willing to let one go, ask for help to become willing.
Ask yourself
Do I want to change these behaviors and beliefs?
Am I willing for my Higher Power to take away all of them?
Read in the Big Book
Page 76, first paragraph (“If we can answer to our satisfaction…” to “…we ask God to help us be willing”)
Sources: A Guide for Working the Steps with Alcoholics (main) (Appendix Three); A Twelve-Step Journey to Self-Transformation; Study Guide to the AA Big Book (reading pages).

steps.name: Humbly asked
steps.wording: Humbly asked Him to remove our shortcomings.

items.x: Humbly asked Him to remove our shortcomings.
Big Book, page 59
In short

Step Seven is the request: we humbly ask the Higher Power to remove the defects that came out of self-will, because they keep us from being happy, joyous and free. The guide closes the inventory session by saying the Seventh Step affirmation together.
We no longer beat ourselves up: we did the best we could with the spiritual fitness we had. The asset side of the inventory shows what was always inside us, blocked by the liabilities.
What to do
Review Steps 1–6 briefly, then say the words when you are ready.
Look at your assets as well as your defects; they are what grows as the defects are removed.
Keep watching for the defects to return, and ask again when they do.
Seventh Step words
I turn myself over to the care of my Higher Power. May all the defects that stand in the way be removed. Please let it be.
As spoken in A Twelve-Step Journey.
Seventh Step affirmation (said together)

I am acknowledging all my past wrongs and all my defects of character. I want to start a new life today. I ask that my inner resources which I have neglected in the past awaken now and guide my life. I now admit these wrongs to my Higher Power and invoke it to reject every single defect of character, now and in the future. Let it be.
Shortened from the guide’s Appendix Two.
Ask yourself
Am I now willing to be willing?
Do I see that I can’t have lasting sobriety unless these defects are removed?
Read in the Big Book
Page 76, second paragraph (“When ready, we say…” to “…We have then completed Step Seven”)
Seventh Step prayer, page 76
Sources: A Guide for Working the Steps with Alcoholics (main); A Twelve-Step Journey to Self-Transformation; Study Guide to the AA Big Book (reading pages).

steps.name: Made a list
steps.wording: Made a list of all persons we had harmed, and became willing to make amends to them all.

items.x: Made a list of all persons we had harmed, and became willing to make amends to them all.
Big Book, page 59
In short

Step Eight is more than a list: it is the willingness to go to the people we harmed and repair the damage. We can’t know what repair is needed until we understand the harm, so we “get into that person’s shoes.”

Only you have the key to the part of someone’s heart your actions closed. Forgiving others frees you too: refusing to forgive means living the harm over and over. Many who go back out stop after Step Eight.
What to do
Write the names of everyone you harmed, using your inventory as a starting point.
Next to each name, write what you took or damaged: money, trust, peace of mind.
Become willing to go to every one of them in person; a letter only if a visit is truly impossible.
Ask yourself
Have I harmed people, taken things that were not mine, or broken relationships that need mending?
Am I willing to go on to Step Nine and make all the amends?
Read in the Big Book
Page 76 (“Now we need more action…” to “…any length for victory over alcohol”)
Sources: A Guide for Working the Steps with Alcoholics (main); Study Guide to the AA Big Book (reading pages).

steps.name: Made direct amends
steps.wording: Made direct amends to such people wherever possible, except when to do so would injure them or others.

items.x: Made direct amends to such people wherever possible, except when to do so would injure them or others.
Big Book, page 59
In short

Amends sweep away the debris of living on self-will. They are simple: one person going to another and saying, “Here’s what I did, and I am sorry. How can I make this right? Is there anything else we need to discuss?” How they react is not the point.

The guide notes that “others” in this step does not mean you. The Ninth Step Promises come true before we are halfway through. Dr. Bob, after his last drunk, made all his amends in one day and never drank again.
What to do
Beside each name, write the action that will set the harm right, and go over it with the person taking you through.
Make at least one amends today, then call someone and talk it over.
If it helps, role-play an amends first, both accepted and refused.
Ask the Higher Power within for the strength to finish all of them.
Ask yourself
Am I treating amends as a matter of life or death (“to drink is to die”)?
Is there one amends I can make before I go to bed tonight?
Read in the Big Book
Pages 76–83 (“Probably there are still some misgivings…” to “…we don’t crawl before anyone”)
The Promises, pages 83–84
Sources: A Guide for Working the Steps with Alcoholics (main); Study Guide to the AA Big Book (reading pages).

steps.name: Continued to take inventory
steps.wording: Continued to take personal inventory and when we were wrong promptly admitted it.

items.x: Continued to take personal inventory and when we were wrong promptly admitted it.
Big Book, page 59
In short

Self-will returns, so Step Ten practices all the steps daily: watch for selfishness, dishonesty, resentment and fear; set right new mistakes quickly; stay close to others doing the work; and help others. Steps 4 and 5 were a moral inventory; Step 10 is an ongoing personal one.

The reward is the Tenth Step Promise: sanity returns, we react sanely and normally to alcohol, and it happens “automatically” as long as we stay spiritually fit. We are not cured; we have a daily reprieve.
What to do
Before every word or action: Pause. Ask whether it will be kind or mean, selfish or giving. Turn to the better thought.
Test the first thought: could it harm me or others? Would I have to be dishonest? Is it selfish? If yes, it is the ego, so stop.
Look for the second, opposite thought; it is often the true one.
Talk things over with someone who is doing the work, for a second opinion.
Ask yourself
Will I keep taking daily inventory, set right new mistakes as I go, and rework the steps when I become restless, irritable or discontented?
Read in the Big Book
Pages 84–85 (“This thought brings us to Step Ten…” to “…that means more action”)
Sources: A Guide for Working the Steps with Alcoholics (main); Study Guide to the AA Big Book (reading pages).

steps.name: Prayer and meditation
steps.wording: Sought through prayer and meditation to improve our conscious contact with God as we understood Him, praying only for knowledge of His will for us and the power to carry that out.

items.x: Sought through prayer and meditation to improve our conscious contact with God as we understood Him, praying only for knowledge of His will for us and the power to carry that out.
Big Book, page 59
In short

Freedom from insanity is the reward of daily work. In Step Eleven we seek inner guidance, the “vital sixth sense,” so our thinking is directed by inspiration instead of old ideas. The founders kept a morning quiet time, and over time spent less time asking and more time listening.
We have to wake up spiritually each day, just as we wake up physically each morning. We drink only when we are not spiritually fit.
What to do
Morning: get up a little early, read something peaceful, then sit quietly and listen. Write down any thoughts, signs or images that come.
During the day: pause and ask for the right thought.
