Find quiet moments at the day’s stress points (the drive in, midday, coming home).
Night: review your day. Was I resentful, selfish, dishonest or afraid? Do I owe an apology? Was I kind? What could I have done better?
From the guide’s morning meditation

I ask the higher power within to relieve me of all my fears, worries, and doubts and turn over all decision-making to the Right Mind within. In all my relations, I ask for inner guidance to take over.
From the guide’s Appendix C (Guide to Meditation and Guidance).
Ask yourself
Am I willing to commit to a positive daily routine of morning reading, meditation and writing, and a few minutes of evening review?
Read in the Big Book
Pages 85–88 (“Step Eleven suggests prayer and meditation…” to the end of Chapter 6)
Sources: A Guide for Working the Steps with Alcoholics (main) (including Appendices B and C); Study Guide to the AA Big Book (reading pages).

steps.name: Carry the message
steps.wording: Having had a spiritual awakening as the result of these steps, we tried to carry this message to alcoholics, and to practice these principles in all our affairs.

items.x: Having had a spiritual awakening as the result of these steps, we tried to carry this message to alcoholics, and to practice these principles in all our affairs.
Big Book, page 60
In short

Having made conscious contact, we have something to share. “Practical experience shows that nothing will so much insure immunity from drinking as intensive work with other alcoholics.” The guide adds that the goal is not to cling to a sponsor but to depend on the guidance within, and to start taking others through the steps right away.
“These principles” are the steps themselves, practiced in all our affairs for the rest of our lives. This is our first trip through the steps, not our last.
What to do
Find alcoholics and take them through the steps; read a guide together, one evening a week, like a book study.
Offer to help through treatment centers, halfway houses, jails, churches and doctors.
Keep the morning quiet time and evening review without fail.
Retake the steps as a refresher, and write regular inventory, because the ego comes back.
Watch out for letting meeting attendance stand in for doing the work.
Ask yourself
Will I carry this message to other alcoholics and practice these principles in all my affairs?
Read in the Big Book
Chapter 7, Working with Others (pages 89–103)
Sources: A Guide for Working the Steps with Alcoholics (main) (including “The Twelve Steps to Staying Happy, Joyous, Free, Sober and Sane”); Study Guide to the AA Big Book (reading pages).

stepsIntro.lead: Each of the Twelve Steps will offer suggested readings and questions. Don't rush to answer; sit with the questions. Use the questions as a meditation, waiting for the answer to come to you, not from you. My very best thinking got me here; my very best thinking got me to pick up a drink over and over even though I knew it was destructive, even after I had promised myself I would never do this again. So before you start, say a simple prayer: “My Creator, please take from me what I think I know, open my heart and my mind and allow me to see the truth.” The words are not as important as the intent; feel this in your core.

items.x: These summaries are drawn from the Big Book of Alcoholics Anonymous, personal experience and historic guides for working the steps with alcoholics. Guides which describe how the early members took newcomers through all twelve steps in a few sessions: Steps 1–3, then 4–7, then 8–9, then 10–12. A Twelve-Step Journey to Self-Transformation and the Study Guide to the AA Big Book add some points and the Big Book reading pages are just some of the materials I have used.

I have seen hundreds maybe thousands of people come to Alcoholics Anonymous meetings only to relapse. I have never seen anyone who has worked the steps and continued to apply the clear directions of Alcoholics Anonymous return to drinking. Please do this; it will reward you beyond your imagination. You will have freedom, peace of mind and happiness. You will be of use to the people around you. May God bless you on your journey.
